title: Enron: a pipeline giant that wants to trade gas
what: Enron, the Houston company formed in 1985 by the merger of Houston Natural Gas and InterNorth, owns one of the largest natural gas pipeline networks in the United States, more than 36,000 miles of pipe. Chairman Kenneth Lay is adding power plants and has started a 'Gas Bank' that lets producers and buyers lock in gas supplies and prices years ahead. The company is still living down 1987, when traders at its oil-trading unit in Valhalla, New York, ran up losses that Enron put at $85 million.
why: Listing beat: why someone would buy a steady pipeline stock with a new trading idea. The Valhalla affair is the first hidden loss in the story: the true figure, $142-190 million, only came out in 1993.

title: Enron may count future gas profits today
what: The Securities and Exchange Commission has accepted Enron's use of mark-to-market accounting for its natural gas trading contracts. Instead of booking profit as gas is delivered over many years, Enron can now count its estimate of a long-term contract's value as income in the quarter the deal is signed.
why: The accounting choice that made Enron's earnings depend on its own estimates of the future; it powered the reported growth of the 1990s and later hid losses. The approval is dated 30 January 1992 in Wikipedia; how widely it was reported that month is not established.

title: Enron's giant power station in England starts up
what: Enron's Teesside power station near Middlesbrough in north-east England has been commissioned after 29 months of construction. With 1,875 megawatts it is the largest gas-fired combined-cycle plant in Europe and can supply almost 3% of the electricity of England, Wales and Scotland.
why: The showcase of Enron International, which went on to build plants around the world and by 1996 earned a quarter of the group's profit.

title: Enron to buy Oregon utility Portland General
what: Enron has agreed to buy Portland General Corporation, an Oregon electric utility, for about 51 million new Enron shares worth about $2.1 billion, plus about $1.1 billion of Portland General's debt. Enron calls the combination the nation's largest integrated natural gas and electricity company, with 5,900 megawatts of generating capacity and 37,000 miles of pipeline.
why: The utility gave Enron a foothold in the western power market and in California, where deregulation was coming; Enron sold it again in its last months.

title: Enron bids for Britain's Wessex Water
what: Enron is forming a global water company and has made an all-cash offer for Wessex Water, a British water utility, valued at about $2.9 billion. Enron believes water is the next utility market to be opened to competition.
why: Wessex became the core of Azurix, floated in 1999 and a heavy loss-maker; its write-down was part of the October 2001 charges.

title: Enron's profit up 18% as trading booms
what: Enron's first-quarter net income rose 18% to $253 million, or 68 cents a share, from $214 million a year earlier. Earnings from selling gas and power and managing the contracts rose 74% to $224 million, and chairman Kenneth Lay said he expects 1999 to be another excellent year for earnings and shareholder returns.
why: The trading machine was now the profit engine, and the market began to pay a growth-stock price for it.

title: Enron floats its water business, Azurix
what: Enron sold part of its water company Azurix, built around Britain's Wessex Water, to the public in a stock market listing in June.
why: Azurix struggled at once (British regulators ordered price cuts, the Buenos Aires concession went wrong) and Enron bought the public shares back in December 2000 for $8.375 each.

title: Enron says it will trade internet bandwidth; shares soar
what: At its annual analyst meeting on 20 January, Enron presented Enron Broadband Services, a high-speed network it says is run by software intelligence, and plans to trade network capacity the way it trades gas and power. Chairman Kenneth Lay cited a 700% return to shareholders over the decade. The shares rose by more than half in the month, to a record.
why: The moment Enron became a technology stock. The SEC later charged Jeffrey Skilling with making false statements at this meeting: the network and its software did not exist as described.

title: Enron shares hit a record near $90
what: Enron's shares reached a record of about $90 on 23 August. Rebecca Mark, who built Enron's international power business and ran its water company Azurix, has left after a slump in Azurix's shares.
why: The peak. From here the stock lost nearly everything in fifteen months.

title: Enron denies rumours of a profit warning
what: Enron's president Jeffrey Skilling said on 24 November that rumours of a profit warning were untrue, adding that the company was very comfortable with analysts' forecasts of 35 cents a share for the fourth quarter and $1.65 for 2001. The shares fell about a fifth in November as the market slid and as Wall Street worried about California's power market, where a leading utility analyst suspended his ratings on energy companies in October.
why: The first crack. A short-seller, Jim Chanos, started betting against Enron this month after reading its annual report.

title: Skilling to become Enron's chief executive
what: Enron's board elected Jeffrey Skilling chief executive from 12 February 2001, with Kenneth Lay remaining chairman; Skilling said Lay had put rumours of a move to Washington to rest. Enron had revenues of $40 billion in 1999 and $60 billion in the first nine months of 2000. It also agreed to buy back the public shares of its water company Azurix at $8.375 each.
why: The relief rally took the stock back above $80 at the year end, when the company was valued at about 70 times earnings.

title: Skilling takes over; 'most innovative' for the sixth year
what: Jeffrey Skilling took over as Enron's chief executive on 12 February. Fortune magazine named Enron America's most innovative company for the sixth year in a row.
why: Peak reputation. The questions began in the press within weeks.

title: Fortune asks: is Enron overpriced?
what: In an article headlined 'Is Enron Overpriced?', Fortune's Bethany McLean asked how Enron justifies a share price of 55 times earnings when analysts and investors cannot say how it makes its money; she pointed to rising debt and erratic cash flow. Finance chief Andrew Fastow told the magazine Enron does not want anyone to know what is on its trading books. On 9 March Enron and Blockbuster ended their 20-year movies-on-demand deal after eight months.
why: The clearest public warning before the collapse: the numbers that later sank Enron were already in its annual report for anyone who read it.

title: Skilling insults an analyst on a conference call
what: Enron reported record recurring earnings of 47 cents a share for the first quarter and raised its outlook for 2001. On the conference call, when analyst Richard Grubman complained that Enron was the only company that could not release a balance sheet with its earnings, chief executive Jeffrey Skilling called him an obscenity.
why: A small scene that told investors a lot: a company that will not show its balance sheet and attacks those who ask.

title: Enron vice chairman Cliff Baxter resigns
what: Cliff Baxter, Enron's vice chairman, resigned on 2 May. In India, the state of Maharashtra stopped paying for power from the Dabhol plant in January, calling it too expensive.
why: One of a string of senior departures in 2001; by August Skilling's would be the sixth.

title: Skilling quits after six months
what: Jeffrey Skilling resigned as Enron's chief executive on 14 August after six months, citing personal reasons; Kenneth Lay takes the job back. Lay told analysts there were 'no accounting issues, no trading issues' and that the company was in the strongest shape it had ever been in. The shares hit a 52-week low; Skilling had sold shares worth about $33 million in the months before.
why: The warning players should not miss: a new chief executive walking out of a 'great' company without a reason. The next day an Enron vice president, Sherron Watkins, wrote to Lay that the company might 'implode in a wave of accounting scandals' (not public until 2002).

title: Enron 'trading under a cloud'
what: Investors are struggling to understand Enron's accounts; one prominent hedge fund manager said the stock was trading under a cloud. The company admits to deals with 'related parties', some of them partnerships run by its finance chief Andrew Fastow. After the 11 September attacks the stock market fell sharply, and Enron's shares lost more than a fifth in the month.
why: The doubts and the market fall came together; the October results turned doubt into panic.

title: Enron loses $618 million; SEC asks questions; finance chief out
what: On 16 October Enron reported a third-quarter loss of $618 million after $1.01 billion of charges on its water, broadband and other ventures, and cut shareholders' equity by $1.2 billion over deals with partnerships run by finance chief Andrew Fastow. On 22 October it disclosed an SEC inquiry and the shares fell $5.40 to $20.65 in a day; Fastow was replaced on 24 October. Enron drew on its bank credit lines to repay $3.3 billion of commercial paper, and Moody's cut its credit rating.
why: The unravelling. Banks would no longer lend while Fastow stayed, and the company that lived on its credit rating was running out of cash.

title: Dynegy rescue collapses; Enron cut to junk
what: Enron admitted it had overstated profits since 1997 by about $590 million and agreed on 9 November to be taken over by its smaller Houston rival Dynegy for about $8 billion in stock. A filing on 19 November showed about $9 billion of debt due by the end of 2002 and warned of the risk to Enron's survival. On 28 November the rating agencies cut Enron to junk, making $3.9 billion of debt due at once, and Dynegy walked away; the shares closed at 61 cents.
why: A takeover offer is not a floor: once the buyer's due diligence found the hole, the deal died and the shares went to almost nothing.

title: Enron files for bankruptcy, the largest in U.S. history
what: Enron filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection on 2 December, the largest corporate bankruptcy in U.S. history, with debts of about $31 billion. It laid off 4,000 employees in Houston and sued Dynegy for $10 billion. Many employees held most of their retirement savings in Enron stock, now worth cents; the shares still trade, but shareholders stand behind all creditors.
why: The exit. The shares bounced from 26 to 60 cents in December in speculative trading, a reminder that a bankrupt company's stock can still move while being worth almost nothing to its owners.
